newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook- Diesel braces for arbitrage.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook- Diesel braces for arbitrage.

text.p: The Asian diesel market is bracing itself for the onslaught of arbitrage cargoes from the West, with the first expected to hit the market towards the end of this week, traders said.
Trading sources said importers had already secured large storage space in Singapore in preparation for the arrival of an estimated 1.0 to 1.6 million tonnes of diesel.
Diesel prices in Singapore are finally expected to buckle under this arbitrage pressure as players count on local firm Hin Leong Trading to withdraw slowly its support from the market.
In March, Hin Leong bought more than 7.0 million barrels of diesel for lifting in late March and April with most of the second-half April cargoes sold seen coming from the West.
Traders said they expected Hin Leong to slow its support in the local market but discounted an abrupt end to its buying spree.

In a surprise move, on Friday, Hin Leong bought 520,000-barrels of diesel at $26.90-$26.90 per barrel for loading in end April/early May, taking its tally to almost eight million barrels since the buying spree started on March 3.
Traders said the unexpectedly large purchase served to underline the undertainties facing the market as players tried to second guess Hin Leong's action.
Most agreed that if the buying spate continued at such a rate, then the arrival of the arbitrage cargoes would make only a small dent in the market.

Already, the arbitrage cargoes are being counted upon to boost middle distllate stocks in Singapore, which according to figures released by the Trade Development Board, stood at a more than three-year low at 4.953 million for the week ending April 3.
In the fuel oil market, sentiment was dominated by crude weakness late last week and traders expected prices to be largely affected by Brent crude movements this week.
A local trader, who has been expected to support the market, bought only one cargo of 180-centistoke grade last week at $100.50 per tonne for April delivery.
Bids and offers hovered around the $100-mark last week.
"The market should be quieter this week over weak crude values, fewer activities from the local trader as well as thin Chinese enquiries," said one trader.
Some traders said they hoped the low level of Singapore's weekly residual fuel oil stocks could support prices.
The TDB data showed a drop of 2.435 million barrels to 8.229 million barrels in the week ending April 2, the lowest level of Singapore residual fuel oil stocks in at least three years.
Recent Indian fuel oil purchase tenders for seasonal demand were also expected to help the demand side.
India has bought three cargoes for April lifting for the upcoming summer and has two other outstanding tenders.

The gasoline market received a much needed shot in the arm when state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp (CPC) bought two unleaded and one leaded 95-octane reformate cargoes in its latest tender for arrival in May.
In its previous tender, CPC only bought one unleaded cargo for April 16-30 arrival.

Traders said the market, facing strong selling pressure, might stabilise slightly this week on fresh support from players looking to cover CPC's requirement as well those stocking up for the driving season.
